A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same human–multimodal-model study of vocabulary, possessives, and demonstratives. The main text, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite substantial reorganization and expanded evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original human production, replication, and comprehension experiments, alongside evaluations and prompting experiments involving seven multimodal models.

after.justification: V2 retains original human results and reports expanded model evaluations, cue-removal ablations, prompt-variation experiments, and additional diagnostic controls and baselines.

M1.justification: The model architectures and core answer prompts are retained. However, v1 Appendix D.3 explicitly requests a second, post-answer reasoning response; v2 Appendix H.2 omits that step while Section 3.4 still mentions step-by-step reasoning. The PDFs do not establish whether the procedure changed or only its documentation.

E1.justification: The three English word-use tasks and human studies remain. V2 adds diagnostic speaker/gazer identification and spatial questions, model testing on human-format stimuli, and absent, empty, or unrelated-image scenarios within the same referential setting.

E2.justification: The seven principal models and existing prompting comparisons are retained. Appendix K adds evaluated empty-image, unrelated-image, and text-only baselines for these models, with possessive-task results in Table 9.

E3.justification: Model evaluation increases from 768 to 6,144 trials per task and from 16 to 128 objects, with revised trial constructions in v2 Appendix D. New cue-removal, prompt-variation, and visual-input controls expand the testing procedures. The Pearson human–model response-correlation metric is removed; the human experimental design is retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds four systematic cue-removal conditions, human-versus-model stimulus checks, object-group sensitivity tests, spatial-reference controls, three prompt variants, and additional visual ablations. V1's response-correlation analysis and perspective/spatial-condition GLMs disappear. Human comprehension and general error analyses are retained in Appendices I–J.

E5.justification: V2 Figure 2 removes model standard-error bars and explicitly identifies model evaluation as deterministic. Bootstrap resampling associated with the removed correlation analysis also disappears. New chi-square object-group tests supplement retained human standard errors and logistic-regression/post-hoc comparisons.

E6.justification: Model scores and prompting findings change, and numerous control, ablation, and baseline results are added. Reported Llama-4-Scout possessive accuracy changes from 88% to 85.7%, and GPT-4o demonstrative accuracy from 69% to 70.2%; these accompany enlarged evaluation sets, not matched-setting improvements. Correlation results are removed, while human production/replication values remain identical in v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 3.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems, proofs, or a new mathematical theory. Revised trial-count calculations and statistical tests concern evaluation rather than theoretical development.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a shared human/model framework demonstrating increasing difficulty from vocabulary to possessives to demonstratives, larger model deficits, and greater prompting benefits for possessives. The renamed terminology and added ablations mainly change framing and supporting evidence.

C2.justification: V2 introduces interpretations about linguistic dominance, limited visual contributions, and differences in models' use of perspectival cues. Its limitations explicitly restrict generalization from the controlled scenario and reject treating the task as evidence of general Theory-of-Mind, social-cognitive, or pragmatic deficits, qualifications absent from v1.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository pointer and explicit prompt variants and cue-removal text/image specifications in Appendices F–G. Existing model specifications, API/local-hosting information, and approximate evaluation time are largely carried over. Documentation of the post-answer reasoning step becomes less clear.

R1.justification: V2 adds positioning against perspectival-motion research by Masis and Anderson and spatial-language benchmarks by Kamath et al. and Liu et al. Additional modality-dominance and cross-linguistic references broaden context while retaining the original word-level pragmatics and social-cognition positioning.

P1.justification: The title and terminology change from reference to perspectival words, the introduction and discussion are substantially rewritten, and task-design sections are reorganized. Five results subsections become three, with comprehension and error analyses moved to dedicated appendices and ablations foregrounded.

P2.justification: V2 combines human and model accuracy in Figure 2, introduces the cue-ablation Figure 3, and substantially redraws the prompting comparison. The comprehension display moves from v1 Figure 2B to v2 Figure 17, and the error display becomes Figure 18. The correlation heatmap is removed, and multiple control and robustness tables are added.

improvement.justification: New tests of perceptual, prompt, and spatial-reference confounds, together with clearer limitations, make the central interpretation better supported and easier to assess. Reporting problems temper these gains: v2 Figures 2 and 18 contain unreconciled accuracy differences, and Section 4.3 attributes possessive-task gains mainly to possessive-error reductions despite Figure 4 showing substantial personal-pronoun reductions, especially for GPT-4o. The net improvement is therefore limited.
